newsitem.title: USA: U.S. machine tool demand rose in April.
newsitem.headline: U.S. machine tool demand rose in April.

text.p: Demand for U.S.-made machine tools rose in April from the previous month, the American Machine Tool Distributors' Association and the Association for Manufacturing Technology said on Sunday in a joint report.
Total demand in April rose 7.7 percent to an estimated $801 million from a revised $744 million in March. In April 1996, demand was $497 million.

"The significant growth in demand reflected in April orders may be an early indicator that Detroit is beginning to place orders with our industry again," AMT President Albert Moore said in a statement, referring to Detroit car makers.
The March estimate was revised up from $721 million reported a month ago.
Orders in the first four months of 1997 were estimated at $2.75 billion, a 22 percent increase from the first four months of 1996, the trade groups said.
Machine tools are used to shape metal in making everything from bicycles to aircraft. Demand for these tools can provide a leading indicator of the pace of manufacturing.

By region, the report said the Midwest accounted for 52.6 percent of national demand, followed by 13.4 percent in the Central region and 12.2 percent in the Northeast. The West accounted for 11.5 percent and the South 10.3 percent.
Export orders placed with U.S. machine tool makers totaled 266 units in April, up from 240 units in March, the report said. Year-earlier export orders were not available.
Total export orders in the first four months of 1997 were 1,087 units, the report said.

The latest figures were from the 11th U.S. Machine Tool Consumption report, which replaced monthly data on U.S. machine tool orders, shipments and exports issued by the Association for Manufacturing Technology.
